questions.q: What happened to urinary sodium when healthy men fasted for a full 24 hours on a controlled diet?
options: It fell, along with chloride, while urinary aldosterone rose
It doubled as the kidney dumped sodium
It was unchanged in every man
questions.why: The one-day fast lowered sodium and chloride excretion and raised aldosterone; the natriuresis of fasting is a multi-day phenomenon that self-limits by day four.

questions.q: What drives the natriuresis of prolonged fasting?
options: A direct toxic effect of fasting on the proximal tubule
Ketoacid anions that must leave the body paired with a cation until ammoniagenesis catches up
questions.why: Sodium loss tracked organic-acid anion excretion at r = 0.891; chronic fasting excretes 120 mmol/day of ketoacid anions, while a 5 % carbohydrate diet raises ketones only 0.62 mmol/L.

questions.q: Why is your first morning urine dark and concentrated?
options: Because you lost a litre of water overnight
Because vasopressin peaks between 04:00 and 06:00 and the kidney conserved water as designed
questions.why: Varying intake between 1.0 and 2.5 L/day moved urine but not plasma osmolality, and an extra 716 mL/day for a week left morning urine unchanged.

questions.q: Over what timescale does the body settle sodium balance?
options: Within one hour of each meal
Days to weeks, with total-body sodium swinging 200 to 400 mmol at fixed intake
questions.why: A single 24-hour urine classified a 3 g salt difference only 49 % of the time; a 43.5 mmol sachet sits inside the body's own day-to-day noise.

questions.q: Roughly how much sodium does a temperate one-hour session of brisk walking, running or cycling cost?
options: About half a gram, at 0.7 L/h and 34 mmol/L
About 3 g, a teaspoon of salt
questions.why: In 285 adults the mean sweat rate was 0.71 L/h at an estimated whole-body 34.1 mmol/L, a 0.78 % mass loss.

questions.q: How much sodium does a sedentary adult lose through the skin in a day?
options: About 2 g, which a morning drink must replace
At most a few tenths of a gram; balance studies recover 86 to 92 % of intake in urine
About the same as a marathon runner
questions.why: After a five-hour sweat deficit the kidney cut urinary sodium to 21 mmol a day; no retrieved study shows an overnight sodium deficit.

questions.q: What happened to the electrically induced cramp threshold when men lost 3 to 4.7 % of body mass and 3 to 4 g of sodium?
options: It did not change, because the cramp generator is spinal
questions.why: A peripheral nerve block cut cramp duration from 55.6 to 2.6 s; the cramp sits in the alpha-motor-neuron pool, not in the fluid around the muscle.

questions.q: What distinguished the 43 Ironman triathletes who cramped from the 167 who did not?
options: Lower serum sodium below the normal range
Greater weight loss during the race
Drinking plain water instead of a sports drink
Faster race time and a history of cramping, with no electrolyte or body-weight difference
questions.why: Prior cramps, pace, muscle damage, sex, age and injury predict cramps across cohorts of 82 to 76,654 athletes.

questions.q: Why does pickle juice relieve a cramp?
options: Through an oropharyngeal reflex that acts within about a minute while plasma is unchanged
By restoring plasma sodium within five minutes
Because vinegar relaxes muscle fibres directly
questions.why: One mL/kg shortened an induced cramp by 49 s with no plasma change; a 1.5 g sodium bolus moved nothing in plasma within an hour.

questions.q: What does the Cochrane pool say about magnesium for the nocturnal cramps a sedentary adult gets?
options: About −0.18 cramps a week with a confidence interval spanning zero, and no trial at all in exercise cramps
questions.why: Intravenous 5 g a day and 900 mg of citrate twice daily were also null; a sachet's 60 to 120 mg is below every dose that failed.

questions.q: What did the Kawasaki spot-urine formula do to estimated sodium intake in people who also had three to seven 24-hour urines?
options: Matched the measured value within 50 mg
Over-estimated it by 1,297 mg a day, over-estimating at low and under-estimating at high intake, bending a linear mortality curve into a J
questions.why: All three formulas did it, and they still predicted death with urinary sodium concentration held constant.

questions.q: In 10,709 adults with at least two 24-hour urines each, what did each extra 1,000 mg a day of sodium carry?
options: A J-curve with risk only below 3 g
Hazard ratio 1.18 for cardiovascular events, with potassium at 0.82 and no J-curve
questions.why: The sodium-blood-pressure slope across 85 trials from 0.4 to 7.6 g a day was approximately linear with no flattening at either end.

questions.q: Does sodium need glucose to be absorbed from the gut?
options: No: the ileum absorbs sodium actively against a 110 mEq/L gradient without glucose; glucose speeds jejunal uptake
Yes: without glucose sodium passes straight through
questions.why: The glucose-sodium cotransport story explains why oral rehydration solution works in diarrhoeal disease, not a benefit at breakfast.

questions.q: What does 'hydrates better than water' actually mean in the Beverage Hydration Index trials?
options: A measurable rise in intracellular water
Less urine over four hours from a litre you did not need; a sports drink and a sugar-free electrolyte drink equalled water
questions.why: Oral rehydration solution left 1,038 g of urine against 1,337 g for water; the effect needs 27 to 52 mmol/L of sodium and has poor within-person reproducibility.

questions.q: Which way does sodium move water across the cell membrane?
options: Out of cells, by raising extracellular osmolality; the retention is extracellular
questions.why: Holding 43.5 mmol of sodium isotonically needs about 0.31 L kept in the extracellular fluid, which is the whole ORS effect.

questions.q: Which electrolyte is the actual shortfall in Western diets?
options: Sodium: most adults are below 1,500 mg
Potassium: US adults excrete 2,155 mg a day against a 3,510 mg target, and higher potassium tracks lower risk in every cohort
questions.why: Only 0.002 % of a 103,570-person cohort met both WHO targets at once; each extra 1.64 g of potassium tracked stroke RR 0.79.

questions.q: What happens to sweat sodium after a week to ten days of heat acclimation?
options: It falls by about 40 %, with conservation starting on day three
It doubles as sweat rate rises
questions.why: Three days of low versus high sodium diet moved sweat sodium only 10 to 12 %, and salty sweat is partly a fixed ductal trait.

questions.q: In 413 Ironman finishers randomised to an extra 3.6 g of sodium, placebo or nothing, what differed between groups?
options: Serum sodium rose 5 mmol/L with sodium
Nothing: serum sodium, weight change, finishing time and temperature were the same
Hyponatremia was abolished in the sodium group
The sodium group finished 20 minutes faster
questions.why: Sodium in a drink only slows the dilution caused by forced overdrinking; it does not prevent exercise-associated hyponatremia.

questions.q: What predicted hyponatremia at the 2002 Boston Marathon?
options: Drinking plain water instead of a sports drink
Weight gain during the race (OR 4.2) and finishing over four hours (OR 7.4), not the type of fluid
questions.why: Exercise-associated hyponatremia is a disease of drinking more than you sweat, and its lethal error is treating it as dehydration.

questions.q: Does sodium supplementation improve endurance performance in controlled trials?
options: Yes, by 5 to 10 % in every trial
Yes, but only in cool weather
No in three controlled trials; one real-race half-Ironman trial was positive and a concentrated pre-load expanded plasma volume
questions.why: 700 mg/h over a 72-km time trial gave 171 versus 172 minutes; 1,800 mg over two hours changed nothing.

questions.q: When is electrolyte replacement during exercise actually indicated?
options: When duration over 90 minutes, heat or sweat at or above 1.5 L/h, salty sweat at or above 40 mmol/L and fluid replacement over 80 % converge
questions.why: A model found sodium replacement unnecessary in all realistic soccer and elite-marathon scenarios; drinking to thirst matched programmed drinking.

questions.q: What did an oral rehydration solution do to the cramp threshold when drunk during hot, dehydrating downhill running?
options: Raised it 6.5 to 13.6 Hz while plain water lowered it 3.8 to 4.5 Hz
questions.why: This is the one real electrolyte effect on a cramp surrogate; it involves fluid replaced in real time during heat, not a drink taken hours before.

questions.q: How much does potassium supplementation lower blood pressure, and in whom?
options: About 3 to 5 mmHg systolic in hypertensive people at 60 to 120 mmol a day; not measurably in normotensive people
About 10 mmHg at 200 mg a day
questions.why: Five days of up to 60 mEq extra potassium did nothing to pressure in 35 normotensive adults; a sachet is 5 to 13 mmol and has never been tested.

questions.q: What did the 20,995-person salt-substitute trial in rural China find?
options: A benefit only in young adults
Stroke RR 0.86, major cardiovascular events 0.87 and all-cause death 0.88, with no excess hyperkalaemia events
questions.why: The 75/25 sodium-potassium chloride substitute lowered sodium and raised potassium together; a 5:1 sachet does the opposite to the ratio.

questions.q: What does a 1,000 mg sodium / 200 mg potassium stick do to a typical day's sodium-to-potassium molar ratio?
options: Raises it from about 2.85 to 3.33, about 17 % higher
questions.why: The ratio predicted risk at least as well as sodium in TOHP, NHANES III and the pooled 24-hour-urine cohorts.

questions.q: What is the randomised blood-pressure cost of a sustained extra 1,000 mg a day of sodium in a normotensive adult?
options: About 1 to 2.5 mmHg systolic, two to three times that with age, hypertension or higher baseline pressure
questions.why: The cross-sectional NHANES slope of 4.58 mmHg compares different people and overstates it; in DASH-Sodium the largest step came below 100 mmol a day.

questions.q: Which magnesium form is the one to avoid, and how do the others compare?
options: Oxide, at 4 % absorption; citrate, chloride, lactate, aspartate and glycinate are not separated by human data
questions.why: Malate's superiority is a rat finding that ranks citrate last; dose dominates, with absorption falling from 65 % to 11 % as the dose rises.

questions.q: How much magnesium does a hard 2.5 litre sweat session cost?
options: About 3 mg, under 1 % of the RDA, at 1.27 mg per litre
questions.why: The reported fall in sweat magnesium with acclimation was a skin-contamination artefact; the positive exercise trials used 350 mg a day in groups of 22 to 25.

questions.q: How does the 50 to 120 mg of magnesium in a sachet compare with the dietary gap?
options: It roughly matches the median shortfall of about 80 to 100 mg a day; it is a top-up, not a repletion dose
It is ten times the daily requirement
It is negligible at 1 % of the RDA
questions.why: Median US intake was 326 mg in Caucasian men and 237 mg in Caucasian women against an RDA of 310 to 420 mg; the serum reference interval is a 1974 population distribution.

questions.q: In which groups does clinically low magnesium actually concentrate?
options: Long-term PPI users, thiazide users, heavy drinkers and people with type 2 diabetes
questions.why: PPI use carried OR 2.0 (7.2 with a loop diuretic) and thiazides OR 2.7 to 3.1, while loop diuretics associated with higher serum magnesium in the general population.

questions.q: Who is at risk of hyperkalaemia from added potassium?
options: Every healthy adult who eats a banana
People with kidney disease or on RAAS-blocking drugs; in CKD G3b to 4, 40 mmol a day made 11 % hyperkalaemic
questions.why: In healthy people the same load produced extra natriuresis within two hours; that response was absent in CKD.

questions.q: What does 1 to 2 % dehydration reliably do, and what does it do weakly?
options: Reliably worsens mood, thirst and perceived effort; cognition pools to −0.14 with a confidence interval touching zero
questions.why: A 4.1 % loss left cognition and balance unchanged while mood disturbance rose.

questions.q: Which hard outcomes does drinking extra water have randomised support for?
options: Recurrent kidney stones (RR 0.45, low certainty) and recurrent cystitis in low-drinking women
questions.why: Coaching 631 CKD patients to drink 0.6 L more a day left eGFR decline unchanged; four cups of coffee a day left total body water unchanged.

questions.q: What sodium intake did the J-curve cohorts actually identify as lowest-risk?
options: PURE 3 to 6 g, INTERSTROKE 2.8 to 3.5 g and Graudal's flat zone 2.6 to 4.9 g; none found 4 to 6 g
questions.why: Every J-curve cohort used a spot-urine formula, and no trial has ever raised sodium against hard outcomes.

questions.q: Where do the reports of sodium restriction raising cholesterol and stress hormones come from?
options: Pooling very short, very large reductions; modest reductions sustained four weeks or more show no lipid change
questions.why: Salt sensitivity is pathophysiologically real but has no clinical test, and the heart-failure sodium trial was underpowered.

questions.q: How does insulin affect renal sodium handling, and what does that say about the overnight fall?
options: It dumps sodium from the proximal tubule
It retains sodium distally at clamp doses, inhibits proximal reabsorption, and a physiological rise in natriuretic peptide cancels it; the overnight fall has never been shown to cause sodium loss
questions.why: Removing basal insulin with somatostatin produced a biphasic, unexplained sodium response rather than a clean natriuresis.

questions.q: What is the evidence that electrolytes fix keto flu?
options: A physiological rationale with no clinical trial; symptoms did not differ between 5, 15 and 25 % carbohydrate diets despite a clear ketone gradient
Three randomised trials showing complete relief
questions.why: The electrolyte problems of real multi-day fasting are hyponatraemia with sodium sparing and potassium, phosphate and magnesium falls on refeeding.

questions.q: Which non-electrolyte cramp intervention has the clearest efficacy, and why is it not used?
options: Quinine, which cuts cramp number 28 % but is restricted for rare serious toxicity
questions.why: The 2024 vitamin K2 trial was retracted and replaced; the TRP-agonist drink has one conflicted positive and one independent near-null.

questions.q: Which potassium salts carry the bone and kidney-stone benefits?
options: Citrate and bicarbonate at prescription doses in specific patients, not the chloride in electrolyte mixes
questions.why: Two years of potassium citrate in 276 postmenopausal women changed neither bone turnover nor density; citrate cut stones in hypocitraturic formers.

questions.q: What does 'cellular transport technology' actually describe?
options: A patented molecule that enters cells
A way to hydrate without drinking
Why oral rehydration solution cuts intravenous drips in children with diarrhoea, not a benefit at breakfast
questions.why: Gatorade measured 327 mOsm/kg, hypertonic under the convention; hypotonic drinks preserved plasma volume best during exercise.

questions.q: What is the evidence that water first thing in the morning boosts metabolism and flushes toxins?
options: One unreplicated 14-person study worth about 24 kcal per 500 mL, and no toxin study at all
questions.why: A better-controlled crossover found no thermogenesis after distilled water or saline, only after sucrose; extra water dilutes urine.

questions.q: Why is over-the-counter potassium capped near 99 mg per solid dose?
options: Because 100 mg of potassium is toxic
Because solid potassium chloride tablets ulcerated and perforated the small bowel; it is a dosage-form rule, not a dose hazard
questions.why: Dissolved potassium in water is a banana's worth; the citrate 'buffer' claim borrows from a 22 g bicarbonate protocol.

questions.q: What does a 1,000 mg sodium sachet do to a typical US day's intake?
options: Takes it to the WHO target
Takes 3,608 mg to 4,608 mg, twice the 2,300 mg chronic disease risk reduction intake, adding 28 % to a 9 g salt day
questions.why: It is 43.5 mmol, about 140 % of an overnight urinary output that was disposal of intake, and it lands inside PURE's disputed reference band.

questions.q: If you keep the drink, how should you mix one stick?
options: In 100 mL as a concentrated shot
In 5 L to dilute the sodium
In at least 500 mL, where it is hypotonic; in 250 mL it is hypertonic and pulls fluid into the gut
questions.why: Keep total supplemental magnesium under 250 to 350 mg, and treat added potassium as a drug if kidneys or RAAS-blocking drugs are involved.

questions.q: What are the real levers for a better sodium-to-potassium ratio?
options: Less sodium and one to two servings of potassium-dense food; potato potassium is as bioavailable as a supplement
questions.why: A sweat test is worth doing only in the long, hot, salty, high-replacement corner, and a patch cannot measure sweat rate.
